thought.text: Let me verify the sink actually logs sessions and that the backend resolves the new sink's IP.

reasoning_content:
The request completed in 118ms with 201, no errors. The OTP row exists (count=1 after the delete... no wait, I ran DELETE 1 and then POST 201, so the OTP was inserted). sendEmail was awaited, and the entire request took 118ms. If nodemailer had connected to the relay and sent a ~5KB message, 118ms is plausible.

But there's no session log on the sink! Weird. DebuggingServer logs each session to the logging module's StreamHandler... let me check: `debug` inside `Server.__init__`? Actually in smtpd, `self.log_message` writes to `logging.info(self._getLocalhostName()...)`?

Hmm, wait — is it possible the backend isn't reaching the new sink? The container's IP is... no, DNS is via alias on the workspace_default network, and the backend is on that network. The earlier `docker exec backend wget http://mailcatcher:1025` got a banner — that was from the old sink (same alias). The new sink also has the alias (connected with --network workspace_default --network-alias mailcatcher). Both can't have the same alias on the same network!

Ah — this is the problem. I recreated smtp-sink with --network workspace_default --network-alias mailcatcher, but the old container's network attachment had already been deleted (docker rm -f also removes the network attachment). So the alias should belong only to the new container.

Let me verify: is the backend actually talking to the new sink? Let me test the banner from the backend: `docker exec workspace-backend-1 wget -qO- http://mailcatcher:1025` → banner "220 <ip> Python SMTP proxy". Compare with the new sink's IP (docker inspect).

Also, a potential issue: nodemailer with an empty `auth: {user:'', pass:''}` — does nodemailer treat empty strings as falsy and skip auth? `if (auth) { ... }` — the auth object exists; it checks `this.options.auth && (this.options.auth.user || this.options.auth.pass)` — both empty strings → falsy → no AUTH. OK.

Wait, let me rethink: nodemailer's default for `secure` is... I set secure: false (port 1025), so it connects in plaintext and tries STARTTLS. Python's smtpd DebuggingServer doesn't advertise STARTTLS. nodemailer: if STARTTLS isn't offered, it just continues in plaintext. No problem.

Hmm, so why is there no mail on the sink, no error on the backend, and the request is fast?

Let me look at the OTP row: was it really inserted on the 3rd attempt? Let me check the _created_at timestamp. If the OTP was created at 22:37:13, the flow passed through the DB transaction, then sendEmail ran (awaited). If sendMail threw, the 500 should be logged. It wasn't. So sendMail resolved → the mail was sent... to whom?

Ah, wait. Could the backend container have cached DNS for "mailcatcher"?! The old sink container was deleted, and Docker's embedded DNS re-resolves to the new container's IP. But Node's DNS cache! Node doesn't cache by default (dns.lookup doesn't cache, but... actually Node 20+ has automatic DNS caching? Node 21/22 added `--dns-result-order`... no. Node 22 has built-in DNS caching for `dns.lookup`! Yes — in Node.js 21+, dns.lookup results are cached (default 30 seconds? `dns.setDefaultResultOrder`... the cache TTL feature: Node 21+ caches dns.lookup for 30 seconds by default). Hmm, that's short.

The new sink started around 22:37:0x, the request was at 22:37:13 — if the backend had cached the old sink's IP (from the banner test at 22:36:5x?), it would try the old IP. Old container deleted → connection refused → ECONNREFUSED error → 500. No 500. So it's not this.

Wait a sec, let me re-verify that the OTP row actually came from this request (22:37:13) and not from before. Let me query _created_at.

And wait — the issue might be this: nodemailer is sending to a `from` of "DaZ-Pilot <noreply@daz-pilot.local>"... no problem.

Actually — wait. I just remembered! Python's `smtpd` DebuggingServer: it writes session logs with `self.log_message` → `logging` → but by default it goes to **stderr**, and I'm capturing that. The 4 lines I saw were stderr warnings at startup (which went through fine!). So stderr is being captured. A session should appear on stderr too. No session lines → no session reached the new sink.

But the backend got 201 without error...

Let me check the OTP's _created_at and see whether the mail was sent at all. Actually, hmm, let me look at the `sendEmail` call again...

Ah, wait. I've got it. Look at the controller:

```ts
if (SMTP_ENABLED) {
    await sendEmail(EmailTemplateId.EmailLoginOtp, {...});
}
```

And SMTP_ENABLED comes from constants/env.ts. What if the backend's SMTP_ENABLED is actually **false**?! The backend logs at 22:35:24 showed `test-email-login` — irrelevant. But the log for the first init attempt at 22:35:44 showed a DNS error → so at that time, SMTP_ENABLED was TRUE and it attempted a connection. So SMTP_ENABLED=true.

So sendMail should have connected. Unless... the mail really was delivered to the old sink before I deleted it? Timeline:
- 22:36:40: 3rd init attempt (201, 198ms) — old sink was running (with the sed pipe, buffer block). At that time the OTP was deleted and re-inserted. The mail probably reached the old sink and sat in the buffered stdout (the sed process's buffer). I did `docker rm -f smtp-sink` — buffer lost. Plausible!
- 22:37:13: 4th attempt — the new sink was running. The OTP was deleted and re-inserted (DELETE 1 confirmed). Mail was sent... where did it go?? New sink logs: no session.

Hmm, wait, was the new sink really up and listening by 22:37:13? `docker run -d` + sleep 3 — asyncore starts immediately, yes.

Could Docker DNS have returned both IPs? No, the old attachment was deleted.

Let me test directly: send mail from the curl container? The curl container doesn't have the SMTP client. Let me test from the sink itself: `docker exec smtp-sink python -c "import smtplib; s=smtplib.SMTP('127.0.0.1',1025); ..."` to see whether a session gets logged to the sink's own stdout (if I can send from the same container, I should see the log). This will tell me whether the sink is actually logging sessions.

If the sink works locally, then the backend isn't reaching the sink. In that case, check what the backend resolves: `docker exec workspace-backend-1 sh -c "getent hosts mailcatcher"` or wget the banner again and compare IPs.

Actually, the simplest thing is: from the backend container, test the banner and compare the IP in the banner with the new sink's IP.

echo "sink IP:"; docker inspect --format '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' smtp-sink; echo "backend sees:"; docker exec workspace-backend-1 wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://mailcatcher:1025 2>&1 | head -1; echo "sink self-test:"; docker exec smtp-sink python -c "
import smtplib
s = smtplib.SMTP('127.0.0.1', 1025, timeout=5)
s.sendmail('a@b.c', ['x@y.z'], 'Subject: selftest\r\n\r\nbody')
s.quit()
print('sent ok')"; sleep 2; docker logs smtp-sink 2>&1 | grep -vE "DeprecationWarning|import asyn|import asyncore" | head -20
